newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Forty countries to conduct 1998 FX survey - BIS.
newsitem.headline: Forty countries to conduct 1998 FX survey - BIS.

text.p: Around 40 industrial and emerging countries will participate in next year's global survey of foreign exchange and derivatives markets to help central banks better monitor activity in the global financial system.

The Bank for International Settlements (BIS) said the Group of 10 (G10) leading industrial nations decided in December 1996 to repeat the triennial survey, which in 1995 showed average daily turnover in foreign exchange markets of $1.190 trillion.
The survey is the only comprehensive gauge of the true volume of the huge and amorphous foreign exchange market.
Past surveys were undertaken in 1989, 1992 and 1995 and each time they showed strong growth in foreign exchange markets.
Over the years the surveys have become more comprehensive in order to capture the use of new sophisticated financial instruments and expanded to include growing emerging markets.

The 1995 survey included the first attempt at gathering comprehensive data on the opaque Over-The-Counter (OTC) market for derivatives and revealed much greater activity in those products than central bankers had previously been aware of.
Next year's survey will include many of the new BIS members -- such as Russia, China, India, Korea and Mexico -- but also non-BIS members, such as Thailand, Indonesia and Malaysia.

In 1989 central banks from 21 countries participated in the survey, which showed turnover of $590 billion. By 1992 turnover had jumped to $820 billion and 26 monetary authorities participated, the same number as last survey in 1995.

"The objective of the reporting is to obtain reasonably comprehensive and internationally consistent information on the size and structure of foreign exchange and over-the-counter (OTC) derivatives markets," BIS said in a statement.
The data is collected by local central banks, but BIS -- bank to the worlds' central banks -- compiles the national results and calculates global activity.

The 1995 survey showed that Britain had increased its share of the global currency market to 30 percent from 27 percent in 1992. The United States was second with an unchanged 16 percent, followed by Japan with 10 percent, down from 11 percent.
Top spot in the currency league still belonged to the dollar, which was involved in 83 percent of deals compared with 82 percent in 1992.
The 1998 survey has been expanded in some areas from 1995, but in other areas the reporting burden has been reduced.

The main difference is that the 1998 survey will only collect data for OTC-traded derivatives and not for exchange-traded derivatives as timely information is already available from the exchanges themselves, BIS said.
Turnover data for the spot foreign exchange market, foreign exchange derivatives -- options, swaps and forwards -- and OTC interest rate derivatives will be collected in April 1998.
The survey of turnover will be conducted on a locational basis, similar to past surveys.

But data on derivatives outstanding will first be collected at the end of June, 1998 to conform with a regular, six-month survey of major banks in G10 countries that BIS is starting to get a better grasp on the size and make-up of the OTC market.

The data on outstanding amounts will be collected on a consolidated basis and include notional and gross market values for derivatives contracts in foreign exchange, interest rate, equity, commodity, credit and other areas.
